title: Intersex Expression: Genetics, Development, and Stress
objective: Document unexpected mixed sex expression without assuming that genetics, a single stress event, or cultural folklore is the proven cause.

terms.definition: Unexpected staminate and pistillate reproductive expression on the same plant under the defined production context.
Capacity for observed sexual expression to change with development or treatment.
Deliberate treatment used to alter flower expression for research or breeding.
Genetic or developmental susceptibility that may require particular conditions to appear.

coreScience: Intersex expression is a phenotype, not a complete diagnosis. Genetic background, developmental stage, hormone signaling, photoperiod disruption, temperature, injury, disease, water stress, chemical exposure, and other conditions may contribute. Evidence for a universal stress trigger or threshold is not available.

Staminate structures can occur as separate flowers, clusters, or exposed anthers within pistillate inflorescences. Timing and distribution matter. Early widespread expression may represent a different risk and biological pattern than a few late anthers. Pollen viability and seed set must be tested rather than inferred from appearance.

Deliberate ethylene-pathway manipulation can induce staminate flowers on XX plants for feminized-seed breeding; that controlled induction is different from unexplained crop expression. Both must be labeled so progeny and stability records are interpretable.
cultivationRelevance: Inspect systematically through flowering and after equipment or environmental deviations. Isolation and pollen-control decisions should follow the facility's risk threshold, not certainty about cause.
Retest related clones and progeny under a documented challenge and control before describing a line as stable or unstable. A single plant cannot separate genotype from microenvironment.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Clone or family ID, parents, generation, seed type, related plants, and prior observations.
Structure type, node or inflorescence, count, proportion, photographs, pollen and seed evidence.
First and last detection, days after transition, inspection frequency, and progression.
Light interruptions, temperature, water status, EC, root injury, chemicals, pests, and equipment alarms.
Isolation, removal, pollen cleanup, related-plant inspection, retest design, and progeny results.

misconceptions: Every intersex plant was stressed: Stress may contribute, but genotype and development cannot be excluded.
One late anther proves the whole line is unstable: Frequency, timing, relatives, and repeat trials are needed.
Feminized seed means intersex-free progeny: Seed type does not guarantee stable flower expression across genotypes and environments.
evidenceLimits: Controlled cannabis studies are limited and terminology varies. Observational crop records can generate hypotheses but cannot prove causation when multiple stressors and genotypes change together.
